answer.label: Not Brené Brown — popularized by Anne Lamott; wording is anonymous
answer.sourceLine: Brené Brown did not originate this line — she quoted Anne Lamott in Atlas of the Heart (2021). Lamott made the saying famous in her 2017 TED Talk and 2018 book Almost Everything, but she did not coin it either: Quote Investigator traces the exact wording to an anonymous sign quoted in Robin Norwood’s 1985 Women Who Love Too Much, and to an unnamed friend Norwood cited in 1984. The originator remains anonymous.

source.heading: The real trail behind the line

docMeta.dd: Anonymous sign, quoted in Robin Norwood, Women Who Love Too Much (1985)

source.excerpt: Help is the sunny side of control.
trail: 1985 — the earliest documented wording. Robin Norwood’s Women Who Love Too Much describes a sign reading “Help Is the Sunny Side of Control” whose creator is unknown; Norwood had already credited the line to an unnamed friend in 1984.

2012–2018 — Anne Lamott popularizes it. Lamott used “help is the sunny side of control” in Redbook (2012), her 2017 TED Talk, and her 2018 book Almost Everything, which is why it is widely credited to her.

2021 — how Brené Brown got attached. Brown quoted Lamott’s formulation in Atlas of the Heart, and the line subsequently drifted onto Brown’s own name across social media — a documented second-hand attribution.
source.excerptNote: As delivered by Anne Lamott in her 2017 TED Talk, where she added: “Stop helping so much. Don’t get your help and goodness all over everybody.” The wording, however, predates her by decades.
source.rightsNote: The exact wording is an anonymous saying — Quote Investigator finds no identified author, only an unattributed sign quoted in Robin Norwood’s 1985 book and an unnamed friend cited in 1984. Because it cannot be tied to a specific authored work as its point of origin, no copyright status can be asserted for the phrase itself; Anne Lamott’s and Brené Brown’s later published uses of it are of course within their in-copyright books.

author.name: Anne Lamott
author.heading: Anne Lamott
author.bio: Anne Lamott (born 1954) is an American writer known for candid, faith-inflected nonfiction including Bird by Bird, Traveling Mercies, and Almost Everything: Notes on Hope. She made “help is the sunny side of control” famous through her 2017 TED Talk and her books — but, as Quote Investigator notes, she was the saying’s popularizer, not its author. The wording is older and anonymous.

misattribution.heading: Who really said it
misattribution.intro: A feel-good, tweetable line, so it has migrated up a chain of famous names. Here is who actually said what.

items.why: Brown quoted Anne Lamott’s line in Atlas of the Heart (2021); social media then dropped the ‘via Lamott’ and pinned it directly on Brown. She did not originate it.
Lamott used the line in Redbook (2012), her 2017 TED Talk, and Almost Everything (2018) — making it famous. But she was quoting an older saying, not coining one.
The earliest documented wording is an unattributed sign quoted in Robin Norwood’s 1985 Women Who Love Too Much; Norwood credited an unnamed friend in 1984. Quote Investigator found no named author.

misattribution.truthLine: Bottom line: not Brené Brown, and not really Anne Lamott either — Lamott popularized an anonymous saying whose author is unknown.

context.heading: Why the line lands
lead: The aphorism reframes unsolicited helping as a socially acceptable disguise for control — the “sunny side” being the pleasant-looking face of an underlying urge to manage other people. That psychological sharpness, plus its brevity, is exactly why it spreads and why it keeps getting re-credited to whichever well-known voice most recently repeated it.

Its true history is a case study in how quotes climb the fame ladder: anonymous sign to Robin Norwood’s recovery classic, to Anne Lamott’s TED stage, to Brené Brown’s bestseller, to a bare name on a graphic.
detailsBody: Quote Investigator also notes the bare phrase “sunny side of control” surfaced as early as 1908 in a Halifax, Nova Scotia newspaper in a political context, and that variants circulated — Linda Ann Loschiavo’s “caring is the sunny side of control” (1987) and Pamela Meyer’s “helpfulness is just the bright side of control” (2000).
